newsitem.title: UK: Scandal-hit Tory faces "white knight" in UK poll.
newsitem.headline: Scandal-hit Tory faces "white knight" in UK poll.

text.p: "Sleaze" looks set to remain a central theme of Britain's election campaign as an ex-minister embroiled in scandal faces an anti-corruption candidate in what was once a safe seat for the ruling Conservatives.

Neil Hamilton was confirmed on Tuesday night as the party's candidate for the Tatton seat in northwest England after 182 local Conservatives supported him and 100 either abstained or voted against him.

"I am extremely pleased at the overwhelming vote in favour of my adoption and it is a good omen for the election," he told a packed news conference after the local Conservative meeting in a 500-year-old pub.

Hamilton has denied allegations that he accepted money from a businessman in exchange for asking parliamentary questions and has steadfastly refused to step down. The scandal has cost his party -- trailing the opposition Labour Party by 20 points in opinion polls -- dearly.

His confirmation as candidate and the decision of veteran BBC war correspondent Martin Bell to run as a white knight, anti-corruption candidate in a move designed to force Hamilton to stand down, will keep the sleaze issue and the question of Prime Minister John Major's leadership at the forefront of the three weeks left before the May 1 polls.
Major's decision not to get involved in who should stand for Tatton, which Hamilton won in 1992 with a majority of 15,860, led to criticism that he lacks authority in his own party.

"The Tatton Tories have snubbed John Major and guaranteed that standards in public life will be at the centre of the debate throughout the rest of this election campaign," Labour's deputy leader John Prescott said in a statement.
"John Major could have shown some leadership, stepped in and told Hamilton he should stand down. Or he could have forced the local party to drop him," he added.

The Conservatives had hoped to shift the campaign away from the issue of "sleaze" -- shorthand for a series of financial and sexual scandals which has mainly hit the ruling party -- but Bell's foray into the political arena made it almost impossible.

The respected 58-year-old journalist, who has reported from the front lines of 11 wars, announced earlier he would stand in the election unless Hamilton withdrew. After hearing that Hamilton had been confirmed, Bell said he was prepared for a fight to the finish.
"He sounds like a nice guy, totally unfitted for politics," Hamilton said after the meeting. "I don't really know what purpose is served by his being a candidate from now on."
The local party meeting in Knutsford was turned into a media circus when journalists descended on the village and television networks hastily erected satellite dishes in the pub car park.
Hamilton had told the horde of reporters awaiting his arrival that he felt more like a rock star than a politician.
Earlier on Tuesday the two men traded jibes in a high noon confrontation surrounded by a forest of cameras and microphones on Knutsford Heath.

Hamilton ambushed Bell, who was about to address an open-air press conference explaining why he had entered the race. Standing inches apart, Hamilton demanded to know if Bell was trying to ruin his political career.
"The irresistible inference to be drawn from that is that you think I am guilty of corruption in some shape or form," he said.
Bell, wearing his trademark white suit, worn as a talisman on battlefields around the world, responded: "I think the issue of trust is important."

Bell is supported by both main opposition parties, who have withdrawn their candidates. His intervention is unprecedented in post-war British politics. Bookmakers say he is 2-5 favourite to defeat Hamilton.
